title: Polynomial kernels for minor-free edge deletion
formal: Does every fixed finite family \(\mathcal H\) of finite simple undirected graphs admit a deterministic polynomial kernel for \(\mathcal H\)-Minor-Free Edge Deletion, parameterized only by the number \(k\) of edges that may be deleted? An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\ge0\). It is a yes-instance if there exists \(F\subseteq E(G)\) with \(|F|\le k\) such that \(G-F\) contains no graph from \(\mathcal H\) as a minor. The kernel must return one equivalent instance of this same problem with total encoding length and output parameter bounded by a polynomial in \(k+1\), as specified below.
why: A polynomial kernel would bound all information relevant to the deletion decision by a polynomial in the allowed number of changes, irrespective of the size of the original graph. This would make minor exclusion a broad source of effective preprocessing for edge repair. The distinction from vertex deletion matters because deleting a few edges can leave all vertices present and does not provide the same structural control as removing a small set of vertices.
status_note: Explicitly open in the 2020 source and retained in the 2023 published survey. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 did not identify a deterministic polynomial kernel for every fixed forbidden-minor family, or an unconditional refutation. Existing vertex-deletion kernels and algorithms assuming minor-free inputs have different scopes.

progress.text: The checked survey version 2 poses Open Problem 2.13 for minor-free edge deletion and distinguishes it from the adjacent vertex-deletion result.
The published Computer Science Review article retains the polynomial-kernel question as Open Problem 2.13 on printed page 8.

Bandyapadhyay and coauthors study robust contraction decompositions and algorithmic applications on minor-free input graphs. Their result has a different promise and does not furnish a kernel for deleting edges to reach an arbitrary excluded-minor family.

category_assignment.reason: Topic of the imported textbook or survey question

importance.reason: A broad kernelization question for structural graph repair, encompassing planarization and arbitrary fixed forbidden-minor families. It tests whether fixed-parameter tractability can be strengthened to polynomial preprocessing for edge modifications, a substantially different setting from established vertex-deletion results.

sentences: The problem deletes at most k edges so that the remaining graph excludes every member of a fixed forbidden-minor family.
It asks whether every such family permits a polynomial-time reduction to one equivalent instance of polynomial size in k.
The input graph is arbitrary, and all vertices remain available during edge deletion.
A general kernel would provide a broad preprocessing guarantee for structural graph repair beyond known fixed-parameter algorithms.
The card restores the family quantifier and distinguishes vertex deletion, promised minor-free inputs and more general compressions.

definitions: A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges; after contraction, loops are discarded and parallel edges are merged. These operations define containment only. In the deletion problem itself, the permitted modifications are deletions of original edges: \(G-F\) retains every vertex. A graph is \(\mathcal H\)-minor-free when no \(H\in\mathcal H\) is its minor. Families and their graphs may be disconnected; no member is required to be planar. The empty family and empty graphs are allowed under the stated minor definition, including their trivial cases. The family is fixed before the input graph and budget and is not counted as an input parameter. Graph \(G\) has labelled vertices \([n]\), possibly \(n=0\), and is encoded by a length-delimited binary integer \(n\) and its upper-triangular adjacency-bit array. The budget is a length-delimited binary integer \(k\); let \(L\) be the total input bit length. A polynomial kernel for fixed \(\mathcal H\) means that there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine \(A_{\mathcal H}\), constants \(C_{\mathcal H}\ge1\), and integers \(b_{\mathcal H},d_{\mathcal H}\ge1\) such that for every \((G,k)\) it outputs a graph \(G^{\prime}\) and integer \(k^{\prime}\ge0\) in at most \(C_{\mathcal H}(L+2)^{b_{\mathcal H}}\) bit steps, with \[(G,k)\text{ is yes}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ (G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\text{ is yes},\qquad |\operatorname{enc}(G^{\prime},k^{\prime})|+k^{\prime}\le C_{\mathcal H}(k+1)^{d_{\mathcal H}}.\] The output uses the same graph and budget encoding and the same fixed forbidden family. The machine has a fixed finite number of tapes and a finite alphabet, with initially blank work tapes; input, output and all preprocessing are charged. No randomness, oracle, graph-dependent advice, extra weights or annotations, or calls to an instance-solving oracle are allowed. Constants and the finite program may depend on the entire fixed family, but not on \(G\) or \(k\); a uniform procedure compiling an arbitrary family into its kernel is not additionally required. Input graphs have no promise of being minor-free initially. The parameter bound includes \(k=0\) through \(k+1\). Binary encoding of very large budgets does not authorize time polynomial in their numerical value; the task has only \(|E(G)|\) possible edge deletions, so budgets above this value are equivalent to that capped budget.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universally quantified kernel-existence statement, or of its negation. An affirmative proof must establish a finite deterministic polynomial-time kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family, together with the equivalence and size/parameter bounds on every input. A negative proof must establish failure for at least one specified fixed family. A result for a family containing a planar graph alone, a vertex-deletion kernel, a kernel on already minor-free input graphs, a randomized compression, or a polynomial Turing kernel does not establish the full target. A kernel with output in a different annotated or weighted problem does not suffice unless the conversion to the stated unweighted problem and its size bound are proved. Conditional lower bounds remain conditional unless their additional assumptions are proved. This is a yes/no preprocessing question, not an estimate of the optimum deletion count.

context_blocks.text: The survey’s notation uses a family of forbidden graphs, not just one forbidden graph. Its Open Problem 2.13 follows the separate planar-deletion question and concerns removing edges to obtain a minor-free graph. The card restores that family scope and uses minor containment, which is distinct from the induced-subgraph containment discussed elsewhere in the survey.

The source records fixed-parameter tractability for the deletion task, but asks for the stronger polynomial-kernel property. An algorithm with an arbitrary parameter-dependent factor can decide small-budget instances without providing a polynomial-size equivalent instance in polynomial input time.

The 2023 published survey retains Open Problem 2.13. It contrasts the edge problem with kernels for deleting vertices when the forbidden family includes a planar graph. Those vertex results neither remove the edge-versus-vertex distinction nor cover every forbidden family required here.

A kernel must preserve the decision on arbitrary input graphs, including graphs that already satisfy the target property and those far from it. It is not enough to assume the input is minor-free or to return a list of oracle queries. Changes to the graph representation, allowable modifications or parameter must be included in the equivalence and size proof.

The 2025 robust contraction-decomposition result obtains algorithms for several deletion and cut problems on graphs that are already minor-free. Here minor-freeness is the desired output property after modifications, so that result’s input restriction describes a different task and does not settle the kernel question.
